title: The Pitfalls and False Promises of Nonlawyer Ownership of Law Firms
author: Stephen P. Younger

st.t: Market reform: Information and incentives shape access

st.t: Ownership reform: Investment openings may miss justice needs
st.an: The essay strongly supports the synthesis’s central caution that nonlawyer ownership may create commercial opportunities without demonstrating meaningful access-to-justice gains. It also reinforces the distinction between Rule 5.4 ownership reform and unauthorized-practice rules, raises professional-independence and service-quality risks, and favors targeted, lawyer-supported innovation instead of treating ownership liberalisation as the necessary route to access.
qs: 16 As described below, advocates for NLO have not explained how these ABS entities will improve access to justice, and there is no evidence indicating that they have done so yet or will do so in the future.

st.t: Provider reform: Competition cannot overcome every access barrier
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s proposition that opening ownership and increasing competition cannot by themselves resolve the justice gap. It distinguishes unmet legal need from evidence that nonlawyer ownership improves access, argues that claimed benefits remain theoretical, and warns that lower prices may entail quality risks while diverting attention from lawyer-led innovation, pro bono work and public funding.
qs: 94 However, there is no evidence that NLO has made or will make a dent in this crisis.

Because nonlawyers are not bound by the same rules of professional conduct as lawyers, this modest increase in access to legal services through ABS entities likely risks trading lower prices for unacceptably low quality.

st.t: Regulatory sandboxes: Conditional entry tests consumer risk
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s cautious proposition by arguing that early alternative-business-structure adoption does not demonstrate benefits for those with the greatest unmet legal needs and may create unacceptable quality risks. Its risk claims are predictive rather than evidence of realised harm, consistent with the synthesis’s treatment of access and safety evidence as inconclusive.
qs: As discussed further below, these entities are not likely to benefit those most in need of access to justice.

Because nonlawyers are not bound by the same rules of professional conduct as lawyers, this modest increase in access to legal services through ABS entities likely risks trading lower prices for unacceptably low quality.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Younger supports the cluster’s cautious, selective-deployment framing: software can mishandle contextual nuance, consumers may be unable to evaluate outputs, and expanded legal-service availability does not itself establish improved access to justice. His focus is Rule 5.4 and nonlawyer ownership rather than AI work redesign generally, so the support is narrower than the cluster.

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: The source aligns with the synthesis’s account of coexistence and incumbent adaptation: law firms are developing technology-enabled delivery platforms with flexible business models and pricing, while ABS entrants broaden the range of organisational forms. It adds caution about equating technology or nonlawyer ownership with improved access, but does not reject workflow unbundling or selective delivery reform.

kp.k: Retain ownership restrictions to protect lawyers’ independence
kp.d: Younger argues against rewriting ABA Model Rule 5.4 to permit nonlawyer ownership (NLO). He maintains that investors who are not bound by lawyers’ professional obligations could prioritize profits over client interests. This is an argument about regulatory safeguards and anticipated risks, rather than an empirical finding about AI’s effects.
qs: This Essay argues against rewriting Rule 5.4 to allow nonlawyer ownership of law firms.

The purpose of Rule 5.4—which the Comments to the Rule expressly state— is to prevent nonlawyers from interfering with lawyers’ independent professional judgment and to uphold the obligation of lawyers to maintain their independent professional judgment.

kp.d: The essay distinguishes the ABA’s model rules from jurisdictional reforms. New South Wales permitted fee sharing and NLO in 2001; England and Wales authorized NLO through the Legal Services Act 2007. Arizona abolished its Rule 5.4 in 2020 and had licensed twenty-five ABS entities by August 2022. Utah introduced its experimental sandbox in 2020, scheduled through August 2027; its May 2022 report identified forty-one active ABS entities. Younger considers the foreign compliance safeguards insufficient to overcome his concerns.
qs: Arizona abolished Rule 5.4 entirely, while Utah instituted a regulatory sandbox to license ABSs in which lawyers and nonlawyers partner to provide legal services.
Arizona approved its first ABS in 2021, and as of August 2022, the state had licensed twenty-five such entities.
Utah’s May 2022 Sandbox Activity Report identified forty-one active ABS entities.

kp.k: Bar opposition emphasizes ethics and accountability
kp.d: Younger interprets repeated ABA decisions and state-bar responses as evidence of enduring professional opposition, principally motivated by ethical concerns rather than economic protectionism. The 2012 NYSBA survey received over 1,200 responses: 78.4% opposed NLO, and 77.1% would not consider granting ownership interests or, for in-house counsel, would not consider them beneficial. Approximately 73% of California’s 2019 commenters opposed one or more proposed reforms, not necessarily NLO alone. The ABA’s 2022 Resolution 402 reaffirmed opposition while preserving Resolution 115’s support for studying regulatory innovation.
qs: 78.4% of all respondents opposed NLO,
The survey received over 1,200 responses.
Approximately 73% of the commenters opposed one or more of the state bar’s proposals, which included expanding NLO.

kp.k: Investor incentives could distort client representation
kp.d: Younger identifies potential conflicts involving settlements, affiliated financial services, advertising, unauthorized practice, confidentiality and conflicts of interest. He argues that nonlawyer owners may favor fee-generating settlements over continued litigation in clients’ interests. His discussion of Trajan Estate raises concerns about incentives to refer estate-planning clients to an affiliated financial adviser; it does not report an adjudicated instance of misconduct.
qs: For example, nonlawyer owners of law firms, who are not bound by legal-ethics rules, may be incentivized to push for a settlement in which they have an interest in sharing fees rather than continuing litigation to obtain the best result for the client.
Moreover, the lawyers at Trajan Estate have every financial incentive to steer their clients to the affiliated investment advisor—whether it benefits their clients or not.

kp.k: Chatbots and self-service documents raise contextual-advice concerns
kp.d: Discussing 1Law’s chatbot and software-facilitated document services, Younger argues that consumers may ask complex questions, misunderstand whether a lawyer is involved, or fail to recognize circumstances requiring contextual advice. He contrasts a chatbot’s potentially literal divorce answer with a lawyer’s inquiry into individual circumstances. These are asserted risks and an illustrative hypothetical, not measured chatbot performance or evidence about generative-model hallucinations.
qs: For example, if a consumer asked, “Do I need a lawyer to get a divorce?” the chatbot might simply explain that a person is permitted to proceed through divorce litigation without a lawyer.

Here, again, lawyers have recognized the risk that consumers—particularly those least familiar with the legal system—will not be equipped to properly utilize this sort of software and will lack the information needed to adequately evaluate their legal needs such that the resulting legal documents may not be suited to the person’s circumstances.

kp.k: Access-to-justice benefits remain unproven, Younger argues
kp.d: Younger defines access to justice primarily as free or low-cost assistance for indigent people, particularly courtroom representation, rather than any expansion of legal services. Drawing on commentary about the United Kingdom and Australia and descriptions of Arizona and Utah licensees, he argues that NLO has not demonstrably narrowed this gap. He characterizes many approved businesses as targeting commercial, financial or document-preparation needs rather than underserved litigation. His broader conclusion that reform will not resolve the gap goes beyond the reported absence of demonstrated benefits.
qs: Advocates of NLO have not presented any compelling evidence that NLO will improve access to justice in a meaningful way.
Despite being early adopters of NLO reform, there is no clear evidence that low- and moderate-income populations in the United Kingdom or Australia have received greater access to legal services.
As noted above, the vast majority of ABS entities licensed in Arizona or Utah do not offer to represent indigent clients in court.

kp.k: Personal-injury investment may duplicate existing affordable access
kp.d: Younger argues that ABS investment in personal-injury and mass-tort practices targets areas already served through contingency fees rather than the largest unmet needs. Citing research on the United Kingdom, he reports that ABS firms held 33.5% of the personal-injury market between 2012 and 2013, while 79% of people bringing personal-injury matters in England and Wales had not paid their solicitor before ABS licensing because other payment arrangements existed. He uses these figures to question the incremental access benefits of ownership reform.
qs: ABS firms licensed in the United Kingdom have been disproportionately concentrated in certain sectors, particularly the personal-injury field, where— between 2012 and 2013—ABS firms accounted for 33.5% of the market share.

Before ABS entities were licensed in the United Kingdom, “[79%] of those who brought a personal injury matter in England and Wales reported they did not pay for their solicitor because the solicitor was compensated by their insurance company, was contracted under a no win no fee arrangement, or was provided through legal aid, a trade union, or some other source.”

kp.k: Innovation need not require external ownership
kp.d: Younger disputes proponents’ claim that NLO is necessary for innovation. He cites online dispute resolution, virtual courts, streamlined processes, navigator programs and lawyer-supported online advice as alternatives under existing rules. He also cites Cleary Gottlieb’s June 2022 launch of ClearyX as an example of technology-enabled service redesign within a law firm. His suggestion that experience with such systems can extend to pro bono work is prospective, not a demonstrated access outcome.
qs: In fact, lawyers and nonlawyers are already working together—under existing ethics rules—to innovate legal services.

Examples include online dispute resolution, new tools and forms of assistance for pro se litigants, expanded virtual court services, streamlined litigation processes, technology to facilitate pro bono work, and technology and innovation to help lawyers deliver their services more efficiently.
As lawyers gain experience with programs like ClearyX, they will be able to apply this innovative technology to all aspects of their practice, including pro bono services.

kp.k: Existing rules permit supervised nonlawyer participation
kp.d: Younger argues that existing ethics rules already accommodate nonlawyer executives, incentive compensation, overall profit sharing, supervised paraprofessional work and outsourced support services. He distinguishes overall firm-profit incentives from case-specific fee sharing and stresses that lawyers must retain supervision and responsibility. This supports his preference for technology and nonlawyers complementing lawyer-led delivery rather than controlling the practice.
qs: Under current ethics rules, law firms can already provide incentive compensation to and share overall profits with such nonlawyer managers.

This Rule does not prohibit a lawyer from employing the services of paraprofessionals and delegating functions to them, so long as the lawyer supervises the delegated work and retains responsibility for their work.
Nor does the rule prohibit outsourcing support services, such as document review or due diligence.

kp.k: Targeted public and professional programs are preferred
kp.d: Younger favors expanded pro bono services, public funding, right-to-counsel initiatives, navigator programs and lawyer-delivered online advice. He cites a 2018 ABA report finding that eighty-one percent of attorneys had provided pro bono services during their careers and reports that New York City eviction representation increased from 1 percent to 40 percent following right-to-counsel legislation. He also highlights contingency and flat fees as existing affordability mechanisms and argues that closing the justice gap is a governmental and societal responsibility, not exclusively lawyers’ duty.
qs: According to a 2018 ABA report, eighty-one percent of attorneys have provided pro bono services at some point in their careers.

For example, NYSBA has “supported the New York City Council’s ‘Right to Counsel’ legislation that provides free legal representation in eviction cases—a move that increased representation in Housing Court from 1 percent to 40 percent.”
That is because these are societal problems that require action on a much broader scale and are, thus, the responsibility of federal, state, and local governments.

kp.k: Few complaints do not establish consumer safety
kp.d: Younger rejects low complaint counts as sufficient evidence that NLO is safe. He reports eleven complaints to Utah’s Office of Legal Services Innovation as of June 2022, with fewer classified as harm-related. To support his underreporting argument, he cites 2018 ABA data showing public discipline of less than one-quarter of one percent of actively licensed practicing lawyers in forty-five states and the District of Columbia. His conclusion is that complaint scarcity does not resolve concerns about inherent conflicts.
qs: For example, as of June 2022, Utah disclosed that there had been only eleven complaints reported to the Office of Legal Services Innovation, and even fewer were harmrelated complaints.
Thus, the lack of major consumer complaints clearly does not mean that NLO services are unaffected by the inherent conflicts that they face.

kp.k: Large ABS competitors could displace community firms
kp.d: Younger reports and endorses lawyers’ concern that well-funded, nonlawyer-controlled ABS entities could undercut smaller firms, including rural practices, and leave communities with fewer locally embedded lawyers. This is a predicted competitive effect rather than a documented displacement outcome. He links it to his broader objection that increasing supply and lowering prices do not adequately address service quality and professional responsibility.
qs: Their concern is that allowing NLO will result in large, well-funded ABS entities controlled by nonlawyers that will simply drive out of business smaller law firms that have well-trained lawyers, are often located in (and integral to) smaller or rural communities and are unable to compete with large corporations.
Allowing this would leave markets with few lawyers who are integral participants in their communities.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Younger argues that consumer-facing chatbots and software cannot replace context-sensitive lawyer advice safely, while lawyer-led technology can improve delivery without requiring nonlawyer ownership.
pts.d: The essay primarily addresses nonlawyer ownership rather than AI specifically. Its relevant claims concern chatbots, software-assisted legal documents, and technology-enabled service delivery; it does not identify these systems as generative AI. Younger argues that 1Law cannot prevent complex questions, ensure consumers understand that its chatbot is not operated by a lawyer, or teach it to respond to legal nuance. His hypothetical divorce question illustrates the distinction between explaining that self-representation is permitted and assessing whether a particular client needs counsel. He further argues that self-service document tools can leave consumers with documents unsuited to their circumstances. In contrast, he presents lawyer-led technology and ClearyX as routes to more efficient services under existing ownership rules, and predicts that experience with such technology can extend to pro bono practice.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The technology claims draw on provider descriptions, regulatory listings, program examples, and a hypothetical legal question, rather than measured AI performance.
pts.d: On pages 268–269, Younger cites Utah's authorized-entity descriptions of 1Law and LawPal and uses a hypothetical divorce inquiry to explain his concerns about nuance. On pages 277–279, descriptions of Savvi Technologies, Hello Divorce, and Rocket Lawyer support his account of self-service delivery; these are not reported tests of accuracy or consumer outcomes. On pages 284–285, he cites lawyer-supported navigator programs, online pro bono advice, and Cleary Gottlieb's June 2022 ClearyX launch announcement as examples of innovation without ownership reform. The cited announcement identifies ClearyX as AI- and data-driven, but its efficiency and incubation objectives remain announced aims rather than measured results in this essay. No AI benchmark, error rate, or controlled comparison is supplied.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The concerns describe services operating by October 2022; the extension of lawyer-led innovation into pro bono work is an undated, experience-dependent prediction.
pts.d: Younger writes as of October 19, 2022, drawing on the early Arizona and Utah ownership-reform experiments and the June 2022 ClearyX launch. His chatbot concerns apply even where the intended use is answering simple questions, because consumers may pose complex questions or fail to recognize the system's limitations. His document-software concerns are strongest where consumers must identify and manage their own legal needs without adequate lawyer involvement. He acknowledges that some providers offer lawyers for questions beyond software capabilities but questions whether this arrangement ensures ethical compliance. The positive prediction about extending innovation into pro bono services is conditional on lawyers gaining experience; no implementation deadline or quantitative forecast is given.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are legally inexperienced consumers, people unable to afford counsel, small businesses using online services, and lawyers developing technology-supported delivery.
pts.d: Younger identifies consumers unfamiliar with the legal system as particularly exposed to inappropriate documents and insufficient advice. Divorce clients who cannot afford lawyers exemplify the group that may save money while losing contextual guidance. Individuals and small-to-medium-sized businesses using online legal services bear responsibility for preparing documents and recognizing when to seek further advice. For access to justice, Younger distinguishes software availability from obtaining qualified counsel, particularly for underserved litigation needs. His positive examples concern litigants receiving technology-supported lawyer assistance and law firms improving delivery through internal technology initiatives. He frames these benefits as augmentation of lawyer services, in contrast to what he characterizes as commercial providers' efforts to eliminate the lawyer's role.
